name: Authentication and Authorization
intent: Prove who is calling an API, then decide what that caller is allowed to do, and keep the two questions separate.
scenario: A shop API serves customers and staff. Alice is a customer and may read her own orders. Bob is an admin and may list all users. Nobody should be able to pretend to be someone else.
problem: An API on the internet is called by anyone. It must know who each caller is (authentication) and whether that caller may perform this specific action on this specific thing (authorization). Mixing them up, or checking only one, is behind many of the worst security breaches.

howItWorks.title: Authentication: who are you?
howItWorks.text: The caller proves identity once, for example with a password and a second factor, or by signing in through an identity provider (OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect). The server returns a credential the caller can attach to later requests, usually a short-lived access token.

howItWorks.title: The token carries claims and a signature
howItWorks.text: A JSON Web Token holds claims such as user id, roles and an expiry time, plus a signature made with a secret or private key. Any server that holds the key can check the signature without calling a database, which scales well. Because the contents are only encoded, not encrypted, never put secrets in a token.

howItWorks.title: Verify on every request
howItWorks.text: For each call the API checks the signature (so the token was not altered), the expiry (so a stolen token stops working), and the audience and issuer. A missing, expired or tampered token gets 401 Unauthorized.

howItWorks.title: Authorization: what may you do?
howItWorks.text: Once the caller is known, the API checks permission. Role-based checks ask 'is this user an admin?'. Ownership checks ask 'does this order belong to this user?'. A caller who is known but not allowed gets 403 Forbidden. Check on the server for every request, never rely on the client hiding a button.

howItWorks.title: Keep tokens short-lived and revocable
howItWorks.text: Access tokens last minutes. A longer-lived refresh token, stored carefully, gets new ones. This limits the damage of a leak. Revoking a signed token before it expires needs extra state, such as a deny list or a session store, which is the trade-off against pure stateless checking.

pros: Signed tokens are checked without a database lookup, so they scale
Short expiry limits the damage of stolen tokens
Separating authentication from authorization keeps each simple and testable
Standard protocols (OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect) avoid inventing your own
cons: Stateless tokens are hard to revoke before they expire
Easy to get subtly wrong: missing checks, weak keys, trusting claims too much
Key rotation and token refresh add moving parts
Authorization rules grow complicated as products grow
whenToUse: Every API that exposes anything non-public
Token-based auth for mobile apps, single-page apps and service-to-service calls
Ownership checks for any resource that belongs to a user or tenant
whenNotToUse: Writing your own password storage or token scheme: use proven libraries and identity providers
Putting authorization only in the client, where a user can bypass it
pitfalls: Checking that a caller is logged in, but not that the resource is theirs (an insecure direct object reference)
Accepting the 'none' algorithm or not pinning the expected signing algorithm
Long-lived tokens in local storage that scripts can read
Returning 401 when you mean 403, or leaking whether a resource exists

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Holds a token and sends it with each request.

roles.label: Identity provider
roles.description: Verifies credentials and issues signed tokens.

roles.label: API
roles.description: Verifies the token and enforces permissions.
